extracted.intended_audience: general literate public interested in British social and political reform (mid-19th century readers, policymakers, reformers)
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay offering social and political critique of mid‑19th century Britain and its Empire, arguing normative standards for governors, state functions, education, literature, and remedies for pauperism. The text prescribes what good government and public life should be and criticizes current failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial franchise should be select / high money-qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Wakefield ... judges that the franchise for your Colonial Parliament should be decidedly select, and advises a high money-qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and caveat provided: colonies contain a fluctuating migratory mass 'not destitute of money, but very much so of loyalty, permanency, or civic availability' whom it may be advantageous not to consult on major measures. The author notes this might 'help' but questions whether it would 'quite certainly bring "wisdom"'; also suggests excluding the Fourth Estate and emphasizing wise advice over mere parliamentary eloquence as alternatives or complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of what is decided over who decides
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the Colonies, as everywhere else in this world, the vital point is not who decides, but what is decided on!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures that truly advance the temporal and spiritual good of the community must be adopted and 'strenuously put in execution.' Transient clamors can be largely neglected; the moral quality of decisions matters more than the formality or popularity of the decision-makers. Example/anti-pattern: parliamentary procedure that produces injustice remains pernicious even if 'parliamentary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and empower experienced, wise, valiant Governors with tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Contrive to send out a new kind of Governors to the Colonies...An experienced, wise and valiant British man, to represent the Imperial Interest..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific prescriptions: choose a man 'fit' (not a sectional or red-tape appointee), give him due power, keep him some time to learn and apply his knowledge, and avoid treating the post as a nomadic rotation. Anti-pattern: appointing a 'Canadian Lumber-log' or token native who merely signs Acts by rote; short tenures and red-tape appointees undermine colonial governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The State must attack Pauperism—organize labor and drain the quagmire
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pauperism...is the corner where we must _begin_...the State become what it is actually bound to be, the keystone of a most real 'Organization of Labor'..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pauperism is framed as a moral and social disease, not merely a financial problem. Remedy proposed: 'regimenting' paupers into 'Soldiers of Industry' via Industrial Regiments of the New Era, systematic public employment/regimentation, coordination between State and private masters until unregimented workers are only those fit to remain so. The author foresees this as the foundation for regenerating society across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The State should abandon theatrical/obsolete functions and return to essential duties
rubrics_metrics.description: "The State...not a reality but in great part a dramatic speciosity...must come a little nearer the true aim again..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State must cast off ceremonious, obsolete offices and functions ('Defenders of the Faith', pompous ritual) that consume resources and obstruct real work. Instead it should concentrate on making 'existence possible, existence desirable and noble' for its subjects—practical functions enabling life and industry rather than spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must teach wise command and wise obedience—practical virtues over mere classical learning
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wise command, wise obedience: the capability of these two is the net measure of culture, and human virtue, in every man..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of public schools and universities that prioritize 'vocables', classical rhetoric, and 'nonsense-verses' over manly wisdom and practical training. The State should create seminaries and schools that train leaders and followers in industrial and moral command/obedience; Etons and Oxfords in their current form are inadequate for producing such citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: State should recruit and valorize men 'able to command men' and provide a career path
rubrics_metrics.description: "The want of wants, more indispensable than any jewel in the crown, was that of men _able to command men_ in ways of industrial and moral well-doing; that the State would give its very life for such men; that such men _were_ the State..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes active State policy to discover, train, and retain commanding men—offering them real careers (e.g., leading Industrial Regiments) so that talented leaders need not resort to demagoguery or rebellion. The example implies altering social incentives so leadership in industry and public service is an honored and practicable life-path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature should be serious and spiritually nourishing, not mere merry-andrewism
rubrics_metrics.description: "If Literature continue to be the haven of expatriated spiritualisms, and have its Johnsons, Goethes and _true_ Archbishops of the World, to show for itself as heretofore, there may be hope...If Literature dwindle...into mere merry-andrewism, windy twaddle...there will be no hope in Literature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literature's health is treated as a barometer of national hope. The author warns against literature devolving into entertainment and 'feats of spiritual legerdemain' and calls for high-minded, serious literary figures who guide moral and spiritual life. Possible model: 'true' literary authorities rather than entertainers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public life must embrace veracity and purge hypocrisy ('scavengerism')
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated urgings: strip off the 'pontiff-stole' of hypocrisies and falsities; 'a complete course of _scavengerism_ is the thing you need!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: English public and private life is a 'tissue of half-truths and whole-lies' and that mass falsity has led to social rot (needlewomen, workhouses, cannibal Connaught). Prescription: a moral purification—honest professions, public self-examination, repudiation of cant and jesuitisms—likened to a 'Scavenger Age' or Water-Cure to cleanse body and polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and vigorously execute measures for the real advantage of community
rubrics_metrics.description: "That measures tending really to the best advantage temporal and spiritual of the Colony be adopted, and strenuously put in execution; there lies the grand interest of every good citizen..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on execution as well as policy: not only should wise measures be chosen, but they must be enforced energetically. The author repeatedly contrasts mere rhetorical or parliamentary acts with real deeds—e.g., criticizing parliamentary decisions that reward rebels at the expense of loyal defenders—showing that legality or parliamentary form is insufficient if outcomes are unjust.
